meta.title: How it works
meta.description: What happens when you type ai-jail claude: the kernel layers between your coding agent and your system on Linux, the three network modes, and what is different on macOS.

hero.title: What happens when you type ai-jail claude
hero.lede: ai-jail builds a small, closed copy of your system, puts your project in it, and starts the agent inside. The walls are features of the operating system itself, so the agent runs at full speed and cannot switch them off. The network is off, opened to a few named hosts, or fully open: you choose per launch.

launch.title: What happens at launch
launch.lede: It takes a moment, every time, and nothing keeps running in the background afterwards.
launch.alt: Five steps from left to right: your command, ai-jail reads its config, builds the sandbox, starts the agent inside the walls next to the project, and on exit the walls dissolve while the project stays.
launch.caption: ai-jail builds the sandbox new on every launch and throws it away on exit. Only your project keeps its changes.

steps.title: It reads your rules
steps.text: ai-jail trusts your own ~/.ai-jail file. It treats a .ai-jail file inside the project as untrusted: that file can tighten the sandbox but never open it. Flags on the command line win over both.

steps.title: It builds the sandbox
steps.text: ai-jail sets up each layer below before the agent exists. If a config file is unreadable or invalid, ai-jail stops instead of starting with weaker rules.

steps.title: It starts the agent inside
steps.text: The agent, and every script, package and MCP server it starts, inherits the same walls. When the agent exits, ai-jail exits too.

launch.link: All the flags and config keys

layers.title: The layers, from the outside in
layers.lede: ai-jail does not trust any single wall to hold alone. On Linux the agent sits behind five of them, each enforced by the kernel, plus two filters on what goes in and what comes out.
layers.alt: Five concentric walls around a cyan chip labeled Agent. From the outside in: Namespaces, Filesystem, Landlock, seccomp, Limits. Your home folder sits outside all of them, dim and barred.
layers.caption: Each wall covers for a mistake in the one outside it.

items.name: Namespaces
items.is: A namespace is the kernel giving a process its own private view of the system. ai-jail asks bubblewrap to create them, the same small tool Flatpak uses to sandbox desktop apps, and it needs no root.
items.stops: The agent gets its own process list, its own hostname (ai-sandbox), no inter-process channels to host programs, and a network namespace with no route out unless you open one with --allow-host or --network. If ai-jail dies, everything inside dies with it.

items.name: Filesystem
items.is: Inside the namespace, only what ai-jail mounts exists. The project is read-write at its real path, system directories such as /usr are read-only, and the home directory and /tmp are fresh and held in memory.
items.stops: ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, ~/.gnupg, ~/.docker and browser profiles are on a built-in list that is never mounted. Anything written outside the project vanishes when the session ends.

items.name: Landlock
items.is: Landlock is a Linux kernel feature that lets a process give up access to files for good. ai-jail uses it to repeat the filesystem rules as a second allowlist inside the kernel.
items.stops: A mistake or a trick in the mount layer is not enough to reach a path outside the list, and read-only stays read-only. On kernels too old for Landlock, ai-jail says so and continues with the other layers.

items.name: seccomp
items.is: Programs ask the kernel for things through system calls. seccomp is a filter on those calls, and ai-jail uses it to refuse the ones a coding agent never needs.
items.stops: The filter blocks ptrace, mount, bpf, kernel modules, io_uring, the kernel keyring, raw sockets, and TIOCSTI, the call that types keystrokes into a terminal. It is a blocklist on purpose, so compilers and runtimes keep working. The one process started before Landlock and seccomp apply is the small bridge that carries filtered network traffic out, so it alone stays unrestricted.

items.name: Resource limits
items.is: Caps the kernel enforces on how much a process tree may use: 4,096 processes and 65,536 open files, with core dumps turned off. Lockdown mode lowers them to 1,024 and 4,096.
items.stops: A fork bomb or a runaway script hits the ceiling inside the jail instead of freezing your machine. The agent cannot raise the limits again.

items.name: Environment allowlist
items.is: Your shell is full of variables, and some of them are API keys. ai-jail clears the environment and passes only a short list: PATH, HOME, TERM, locale, proxy and certificate settings.
items.stops: Tokens and cloud credentials exported in your shell never reach the agent. You pass one through by name with --env when a task needs it.

items.name: Terminal proxy
items.is: The agent runs behind its own pseudo-terminal, and what it prints passes through a terminal parser before it reaches your screen. The same proxy draws the ai-jail status bar on the bottom row.
items.stops: The proxy filters out escape sequences that touch your clipboard or query your terminal. Inside tmux or zellij it turns itself off, because nested terminals fight over resizing.

egress.title: Three ways to the network
egress.lede: Every launch picks one of three network modes. The default is the strictest, and the other two are flags you pass on purpose.
egress.alt: Three panels, left to right. Off: the agent chip inside a closed wall, a dim barred cloud outside. Filtered: a small gate in the wall leads to a proxy box, which connects to a cyan cloud labeled api.anthropic.com while a second cloud stays dim and barred. Open: the wall's network side is missing and the chip connects straight to the cloud.
egress.caption: Off is the default. Filtered opens a gate to named hosts only. Open removes the wall on the network side.

modes.title: Off
modes.text: The default. The sandbox gets a private network namespace with no route out, so nothing inside can reach the network at all.

modes.title: Filtered
modes.text: --allow-host HOST, repeatable. The namespace stays closed; a small bridge inside forwards traffic to a CONNECT proxy outside, which dials only the listed hosts and their subdomains. The proxy resolves each name once, outside, and dials the address it checked. ai-jail sets http_proxy inside, and a program that ignores it reaches nothing.

modes.title: Open
modes.text: --network. The wall is gone on the network side, and the agent can send out whatever it can read.

rows.linux: The network namespace itself, plus the bridge inside it
rows.macos: One sandbox-exec rule that allows outbound connections to the proxy's port only

rows.linux: Fails. The proxy resolves names outside.
rows.macos: The system resolver is not fenced, so a low-bandwidth DNS channel remains

macos.title: On macOS the wall is thinner
macos.lede: macOS has no namespaces, Landlock or seccomp. ai-jail turns the same policy into a profile for sandbox-exec, Apple's built-in sandbox. The ai-jail documentation says plainly that this is not equivalent to the Linux isolation.
macos.alt: Two panels. On the left, Linux: the agent chip and its project inside five concentric walls. On the right, macOS: the same chip and project inside a single wall, labeled one profile.
macos.caption: macOS gets the same policy and flags behind fewer walls.

rows.linux: bubblewrap, then Landlock, seccomp and resource limits
rows.macos: sandbox-exec with a profile generated for each launch. Apple has deprecated it, and nothing better exists without kernel extensions.

rows.linux: A fresh in-memory home. Your real one is not mounted.
rows.macos: The profile starts with no global reads and then allows only the paths the agent needs, so your real home stays closed.
The host's /tmp, because there is no mount namespace. TMPDIR points at a private folder made for the launch, and that is the only temp path granted.

rows.linux: --overlay-map lets the agent write to a copy
Off by default: a network namespace with no route out until --allow-host or --network opens one
rows.macos: Off by default, with the same two flags. In lockdown it is always blocked, even with --network.

rows.linux: Invisible: own process list, no host IPC
rows.macos: Mach, IOKit and host IPC are denied unless you pass --macos-host-ipc

windows.title: Windows
windows.text: There is no Windows backend. Install WSL2 and use the Linux version inside it, where you get all the Linux layers.

blocks.title: Why these building blocks
blocks.lede: ai-jail writes as little security code of its own as it can. It drives bubblewrap, which is small, packaged by every major distribution and exercised daily by Flatpak, and adds kernel features on top.

rows.verdict: It can do the job, but it is a setuid root binary, and several CVEs come from that design. bubblewrap works without root.
More than 500 lines of security-sensitive code to maintain and patch alone, to avoid a dependency of about 50 KB that receives upstream fixes.
Capable, but built for servers and driven by protobuf config files, and less widely packaged.
Requires systemd, so it fails inside containers and on systems without it.

facts.title: Small enough to read
facts.lede: The whole tool is one synchronous Rust program, with no async runtime, daemon or container image.

limit.title: What the layers do not cover
limit.text: All of this shares your kernel. A kernel or driver exploit is outside the boundary, and so is anything you open yourself: an agent with --network can send out whatever it can read, and an allowed host is trusted wholesale. For code you believe is hostile, use a disposable virtual machine.
